passages.text: Impiety toward him, then, is for a person who is within the discourse of reverence for God to die saying that there is another god besides the one who truly exists—whether speaking of that other as superior, as inferior, or in any way whatever. For the one who truly exists is this one, whose form the human body bears and for whose sake heaven and all the stars, though superior in essence, submitted to serve the one inferior in essence because of the superior one’s form. God has benefited the human being so greatly beyond all others that, having loved the benefactor because of the multitude of benefits, the human being might, by that very love, be able to be preserved even into the second age.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐν τῷ τῆς θεοσεβείας λόγῳ ὄντα
lexical_decisions.chosen: a person who is within the discourse of reverence for God
lexical_decisions.rationale: λόγος may denote discourse, teaching, or profession. “Discourse” preserves the wording without reducing it solely to either private belief or formal religious office.

τελευτᾶν can mean “die” or “come to an end,” while a possible alternative is “end by saying” or “finally say.” The death sense is chosen because the surrounding argument concerns what a person maintains until death and the next section again speaks of dying under a charge.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὗ τὴν μορφὴν τὸ ἀνθρώπου βαστάζει σῶμα
lexical_decisions.chosen: whose form the human body bears
lexical_decisions.rationale: μορφή is rendered “form” rather than harmonized with the more familiar theological term “image,” and βαστάζει retains the concrete idea of bearing.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὗ τὴν μορφὴν τὸ ἀνθρώπου βαστάζει σῶμα, οὗ εἵνεκεν ὁ οὐρανὸς καὶ πάντες οἱ ἀστέρες ὑπέμειναν δουλεύειν
lexical_decisions.chosen: whose form the human body bears and for whose sake heaven and all the stars ... submitted to serve
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main rendering takes both successive occurrences of οὗ as referring to God. The second οὗ may instead refer to the human being or the human body just mentioned, yielding “for the human being’s sake” or “for the sake of the human body.” That alternative is supported by the ensuing statement that the heavenly bodies serve the inferior recipient and by the account of God’s benefits to humanity.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: κατ’ οὐσίαν κρείττονες ὄντες, τῷ κατ’ οὐσίαν χείρονι
lexical_decisions.chosen: though superior in essence, submitted to serve the one inferior in essence
lexical_decisions.rationale: The repeated κατ’ οὐσίαν is preserved symmetrically. The Greek leaves the inferior recipient grammatically substantive; the context identifies it with the human being, but the translation does not insert that identification into the phrase.

lexical_decisions.chosen: because of the multitude of benefits
lexical_decisions.rationale: The preposition εἰς marks the multitude of benefits as the ground or occasion for loving the benefactor; “in response to” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὑπὸ αὐτῆς ἀγάπης καὶ εἰς τὸν δεύτερον αἰῶνα διασωθῆναι δυνηθῇ
lexical_decisions.chosen: might, by that very love, be able to be preserved even into the second age
lexical_decisions.rationale: “Be able” explicitly represents δυνηθῇ, which governs the infinitive διασωθῆναι, “to be preserved.” The ascensive “even” represents καί before the destination and emphasizes that preservation extends into the second age; the less emphatic “also into the second age” remains possible.
